statement: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Among real continuously}\\\textnormal{differentiable f on [0,1] with}\\f(0)=0,\quad f(1)=1.\textnormal{ Find the}\\\textnormal{minimum of}\\\int_0^1\left(f^{\prime}(x)^2+1f(x)^2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x.\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Take g(x)=sinh(kx)/sinh(k). It satisfies the endpoint data and g double-prime=k^2g.

The energy of g is the boundary value [g g prime]_0^1=k coth(k).

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Keep all inverse branches of the displayed rational map. Write its poles and positive weights in the following general form.}

\textnormal{On every interval between successive poles, including the two unbounded intervals, the map increases from negative infinity to positive infinity. Thus each real y has exactly s plus one simple real preimages.}
\textnormal{No pole is a zero of this polynomial. Its roots are exactly the preimages. The coefficient of its second-highest power gives their sum.}
\textnormal{The inverse function theorem gives positive inverse derivatives. Differentiating the finite root sum makes their sum exactly one.}

\textnormal{The branch substitutions are valid first on bounded image intervals; nonnegativity permits the improper limit. A tangent substitution reduces the remaining integral to the standard cosine-power recurrence.}
statement: R(x)=x - \frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{2}{x - 1}.\quad \textnormal{At each pole of R, set the following integrand equal to zero. Evaluate the integral over the real line.}\quad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{(1+R(x)^2)^{2}}.

analyticCertificate: Each pole has nonzero positive residue parameter and the poles are distinct. One-sided endpoint limits and the displayed positive derivative give a bijection on each pole interval. P_y has degree s+1 and cannot vanish at a pole; its s+1 real simple roots are precisely those branches. Vieta plus the inverse function theorem proves the Jacobian sum. The nonnegative transformed integrand is integrable, so monotone convergence on bounded y-intervals justifies the entire improper identity. Near a pole the displayed integrand tends to zero as a positive even power; at infinity it decays as x^(-2m). The cosine-power recurrence follows by integration by parts with vanishing endpoint terms; its base case is the interval length pi.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Keep all inverse branches of the displayed rational map. Write its poles and positive weights in the following general form.}

\textnormal{On every interval between successive poles, including the two unbounded intervals, the map increases from negative infinity to positive infinity. Thus each real y has exactly s plus one simple real preimages.}
\textnormal{No pole is a zero of this polynomial. Its roots are exactly the preimages. The coefficient of its second-highest power gives their sum.}
\textnormal{The inverse function theorem gives positive inverse derivatives. Differentiating the finite root sum makes their sum exactly one.}

\textnormal{The branch substitutions are valid first on bounded image intervals; nonnegativity permits the improper limit. A tangent substitution reduces the remaining integral to the standard cosine-power recurrence.}
statement: R(x)=x - \frac{1}{x + 3} - \frac{4}{x + 1} - \frac{2}{x - 2}.\quad \textnormal{At each pole of R, set the following integrand equal to zero. Evaluate the integral over the real line.}\quad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{(1+R(x)^2)^{5}}.

analyticCertificate: Each pole has nonzero positive residue parameter and the poles are distinct. One-sided endpoint limits and the displayed positive derivative give a bijection on each pole interval. P_y has degree s+1 and cannot vanish at a pole; its s+1 real simple roots are precisely those branches. Vieta plus the inverse function theorem proves the Jacobian sum. The nonnegative transformed integrand is integrable, so monotone convergence on bounded y-intervals justifies the entire improper identity. Near a pole the displayed integrand tends to zero as a positive even power; at infinity it decays as x^(-2m). The cosine-power recurrence follows by integration by parts with vanishing endpoint terms; its base case is the interval length pi.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use a polynomial whose sign is orthogonal to every polynomial of smaller degree. Define the second-kind Chebyshev polynomials by their recurrence.}
U_0(x)=1,\quad U_1(x)=2x,\quad U_{j+1}(x)=2xU_j(x)-U_{j-1}(x),\quad U_j(\cos t)=\frac{\sin((j+1)t)}{\sin t}.

\textnormal{The leading coefficient of U is two to its degree, so q is monic. Under x equal to cosine t, every lower-degree monomial times the Jacobian is a finite linear combination of sine modes of frequency at most n.}

\textnormal{Indeed, the square-wave sign has only odd multiples of frequency n plus one in its sine expansion; sine orthogonality eliminates every lower frequency. Equivalently, integrating separately on its finitely many sign intervals gives the same identities.}
\textnormal{The difference between any monic p and q has degree below n. The sign moment identities therefore give a universal lower bound.}

\textnormal{Equality requires p to have the sign of U almost everywhere. At every simple interior zero of U its sign changes, so continuity forces a zero of p there. There are n such distinct roots; monicity forces p to equal q.}
\textnormal{The displayed next-to-leading coefficient follows by substituting the leading two coefficients into the recurrence.}
statement: \textnormal{Among real monic polynomials p of the displayed degree, let M be the minimum integral below. Its minimizing polynomial is unique; let c be its coefficient of the indicated power. Find the ordered pair.}\quad\deg p=5,\qquad M=\min_p\int_{-1}^{1}|p(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad c=[x^{3}]p(x),\qquad(M,c)=?

analyticCertificate: The sign of sin((n+1)t) has its usual L2 sine expansion with frequencies (2r+1)(n+1). Multiplication by the finite sine polynomial sin(t)cos(t)^j permits orthogonality term by term by L2 convergence, not an unjustified pointwise boundary interchange. The finitely many roots cos(k*pi/(n+1)),1<=k<=n, are simple and interior. The nonnegative defect |p|-p*sigma has zero integral only if it vanishes almost everywhere; continuity on each sign interval then forces the required alternating signs. Consequently all n interior roots belong to p, proving uniqueness. The independent verifier checks every finite sign moment directly in the cyclotomic field, without using the Fourier argument.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The phase is nonnegative and vanishes only at the interior point zero and the endpoint one. Their orders determine different localization scales.}

\textnormal{Near zero put x equal to n to the power minus one over two p times u. Near one put one minus x equal to n to the power minus one over two q times v. The logarithmic tilt is asymptotically constant on each rescaled neighborhood.}
n^{\tau x}=\exp(\tau x\ln n),\qquad n^{-1/(2p)}\ln n\to0,\quad n^{-1/(2q)}\ln n\to0.
\textnormal{Let J zero and J one denote the masses in fixed small neighborhoods of zero and one, respectively.}
\textnormal{Away from both neighborhoods the phase has a positive minimum, so the exponential decay defeats every fixed power from the tilt.}

\textnormal{For the local dominated limits, the phase bounds give an exponential of a negative even power. The residual tilted linear term has a coefficient tending to zero, and can be absorbed into half that negative power plus a fixed constant. This supplies an integrable bound.}
\textnormal{The factor x in the numerator tends to zero at the first well and one at the second. It is bounded, so the same domination justifies those weighted limits.}
\textnormal{The two powers match. The limiting first moment is the endpoint mass divided by the sum of both local masses.}
statement: V(x)=x^{2} \left(1 - x\right)^{4},\qquad w_n(x)=n^{(- \frac{1}{4})x}e^{-nV(x)}\quad(-1\le x\le1,\ n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}).\quad \textnormal{Find the limit of the normalized first moment.}\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\int_{-1}^{1}xw_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x}{\int_{-1}^{1}w_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x}.\qquad\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t\quad(a>0).

analyticCertificate: Choose disjoint fixed neighborhoods of0 and1 inside[-1,1]. The polynomial has no other zeros, so its minimum on the remaining compact set is positive. Near each well its ratio to the leading even power tends to1 and stays bounded below by a positive constant. After rescaling, the tilt remainder is b_n times the local variable with b_n tending to0. For sufficiently large n, |b_n u| is at most half the leading negative even power plus a uniform finite constant, giving a global integrable rescaled majorant. The interior neighborhood expands to the whole real line; the endpoint neighborhood expands only to the positive half-line. Gamma substitution and recurrence evaluate the two constants. Dominated convergence also applies with the bounded multiplier x. Comparing the exact rational relative exponent proves the three requested regimes.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The rule is exact on constants and linear functions, so only the integral remainder in Taylor expansion contributes. Define the interior node and the three weights.}
\textnormal{Interchange the continuous triangular integral and collect the quadrature evaluations. The resulting kernel is piecewise quadratic.}
\textnormal{The kernel is negative near both endpoints and positive in the middle. Its two interior zeros determine the exact absolute integral.}

\textnormal{Choose continuous second derivatives bounded by one that agree with the kernel sign outside shrinking neighborhoods of the two zeros. Integrating them twice gives admissible functions; dominated convergence makes their errors tend to this bound.}

\textnormal{Equality would require the second derivative to equal the kernel sign almost everywhere, up to one common sign. Continuity would then force opposite one-sided values at each sign-changing zero. This is impossible, so the supremum is not attained.}
statement: \textnormal{For real twice continuously differentiable f on the unit interval with the displayed derivative bound, define the quadrature error E. Find the ordered pair consisting of its sharp supremum C and the answer yes or no to whether an admissible f attains it.}\quad |f\prime\prime(x)|\le1\quad(0\le x\le1),\qquad E(f)=\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x-\left(\frac{1}{12}f(0)+\frac{5}{8}f(\frac{1}{3})+\frac{7}{24}f(1)\right),\qquad C=\sup_f|E(f)|.

analyticCertificate: Taylor integral remainder holds for every admitted C2 function. Fubini is valid because its integrand is continuous on a compact triangle. The weight identities cancel affine terms exactly. The piecewise kernel is continuous at the node, and its explicitly factored roots determine its sign on every interval. The L-infinity derivative bound gives the L1 kernel upper bound. When the sign changes, continuous bounded approximations to that sign are integrated twice, preserving the derivative bound and yielding a maximizing sequence by dominated convergence. Equality of the norm inequality forces the second derivative to have the common kernel sign wherever the kernel is nonzero; continuity across a genuine sign change rules out attainment. In the one-sign cases a quadratic attains the bound directly.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The endpoint values are coupled rather than fixed. To find a candidate extremizer, vary the energy quotient while preserving that relation. Define k as the endpoint multiplier.}
\textnormal{The derivative relation is the natural boundary condition: the boundary term from integration by parts must vanish for every variation whose final value is k times its initial value.}
\textnormal{Writing the solution as a combination of cosine and sine gives a two by two homogeneous system. Its determinant vanishes at the following phase.}
\textnormal{A positive candidate is obtained with cosine coefficient one and sine coefficient k. It satisfies both boundary conditions and has no zero on the interval.}
\textnormal{Now prove the bound for every admissible function, without assuming that the formal variational calculation found the minimum. Define the logarithmic derivative v and complete a square.}
\textnormal{The square proves the desired inequality. Taking f equal to the positive candidate makes it zero, so no larger constant is possible.}
statement: \textnormal{Find the largest real constant C for which the inequality holds for every real continuously differentiable f on the unit interval satisfying the displayed endpoint relation.}\quad f(1)=2f(0),\qquad\int_0^1(f\prime(x))^2\,\mathrm{d}x\ge C\int_0^1f(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.

Since k>1, the chosen phase lies strictly between zero and pi/2, so both cosine and sine contributions make the candidate positive on the full interval. Its logarithmic derivative is continuously differentiable and bounded. Integration by parts in the square identity is valid for every C1 admissible f. The coupled endpoint condition cancels its boundary term exactly. The positive candidate itself is admissible and makes the square vanish, proving attainment and sharpness. Reciprocal endpoint ratios are reflection-equivalent and not included separately.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The nonconvex cost has two zero wells. The best lower bound must allow mixtures of those wells rather than apply Jensen directly to the quartic.}
\textnormal{Nonnegativity gives a lower bound of zero. A measurable mixture with the prescribed mean takes the two well values in the following proportions.}

\textnormal{For a strictly mixed mean, put the single interior transition at t zero as follows. Use linear ramps from minus two to minus one on the first interval, from minus one to one across the middle interval, and from one to two on the last interval. On the remaining intervals keep the neighboring well value.}

\textnormal{Attaining zero cost would force the continuous function to take only the two well values everywhere. It could not have either of the prescribed endpoint values; by continuity an endpoint neighborhood already has positive cost.}
\textnormal{Thus the lower bound is an infimum reached by a sequence, and is not attained by any admissible continuous function.}
statement: \textnormal{Let f range over continuous real functions satisfying the displayed range, endpoint values and mean. Find the ordered pair consisting of the infimum of J and the answer yes or no to whether it is attained.}\quad -2\le f(x)\le2\quad(0\le x\le1),\quad f(0)=-2,\quad f(1)=2,\quad\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=0,\qquad J(f)=\int_0^1(f(x)^2-1)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.

analyticCertificate: For means inside the two wells, nonnegativity supplies the lower bound and a two-phase mixture supplies its measurable value. One can approximate that mixture by a continuous piecewise linear function on shrinking transition intervals while enforcing the mean exactly: for a strictly mixed mean adjust a phase length, and for the pure mean one adjust the middle level slightly above or below the well. These adjustments tend to zero and stay inside[-2,2] for small transition lengths; the cost is bounded on the allowed range, so shrinking transitions have vanishing cost. For means above one, the exact tangent-defect factorization gives a global lower bound without an invalid Jensen invocation on the quartic. The explicitly displayed constant-middle recovery function has exact mean and remains inside the allowed range for the stated delta interval; dominated convergence gives its cost limit. Continuous endpoint incompatibility prevents zero cost in the mixed regime, while strict supporting-line equality forces a forbidden constant in the outer regime.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Compare the entire class with the increasing trajectory generated by the reciprocal growth integral. Define the growth function and its increasing integral.}
\textnormal{For an arbitrary admissible u, its accumulated right side is a differentiable majorant v. Monotonicity of the growth function gives an upper differential inequality for v.}
\textnormal{Before the limiting value of G, invert this inequality. It gives one finite bound for every member of the class.}
T<T_*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u(t)\le v(t)\le G^{-1}(T)\quad(0\le t\le T).
\textnormal{To test the critical endpoint, fix any positive N and follow the exact increasing trajectory until it reaches N. Then keep it constant. Define that finite continuous function as follows.}
t_N=G(N)<T_*,\qquad u_N(t)=\begin{cases}G^{-1}(t),&0\le t\le t_N,\\N,&t_N\le t\le T.\end{cases}

\textnormal{Up to the joining time it satisfies equality in the integral equation. Afterwards the right side keeps increasing, while the function stays at N. Thus it remains an admissible subsolution.}

\textnormal{If T reaches or exceeds the critical time, all such truncated trajectories fit in the interval. Their heights are unbounded as N increases, so no common finite bound exists. Evaluate the critical integral by a tangent substitution and the cosine-power recurrence.}
statement: \textnormal{For which positive T does there exist a finite bound B, depending only on T, such that every continuous nonnegative u satisfying the displayed integral inequality also satisfies the displayed uniform bound?}\quad u(t)\le\int_0^t(1+u(s)^2)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\quad(0\le t\le T),\qquad\sup_{0\le t\le T}u(t)\le B.

analyticCertificate: Every continuous admissible u is finite on its compact interval, so v is continuously differentiable and the chain rule applies. The growth function is positive and increasing for nonnegative inputs, yielding the majorant comparison. G is strictly increasing from zero to a finite limit; below that limit its inverse exists and is finite. The exact inverse trajectory is differentiable and solves y-prime=omega(y) before blowup by the inverse function theorem. The truncated trajectory is continuous at its joining point and need not be differentiable there, which is allowed by the question. Its integral inequality is checked explicitly after the join. Therefore individual finite counterexamples of arbitrary height exist even at the critical time itself. The tangent substitution and finite cosine-power recurrence evaluate the positive improper integral; its decay at infinity is z^(-2p), ensuring convergence.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Compare the entire class with the increasing trajectory generated by the reciprocal growth integral. Define the growth function and its increasing integral.}
\textnormal{For an arbitrary admissible u, its accumulated right side is a differentiable majorant v. Monotonicity of the growth function gives an upper differential inequality for v.}
\textnormal{Before the limiting value of G, invert this inequality. It gives one finite bound for every member of the class.}
T<T_*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u(t)\le v(t)\le G^{-1}(T)\quad(0\le t\le T).
\textnormal{To test the critical endpoint, fix any positive N and follow the exact increasing trajectory until it reaches N. Then keep it constant. Define that finite continuous function as follows.}
t_N=G(N)<T_*,\qquad u_N(t)=\begin{cases}G^{-1}(t),&0\le t\le t_N,\\N,&t_N\le t\le T.\end{cases}

\textnormal{Up to the joining time it satisfies equality in the integral equation. Afterwards the right side keeps increasing, while the function stays at N. Thus it remains an admissible subsolution.}

\textnormal{If T reaches or exceeds the critical time, all such truncated trajectories fit in the interval. Their heights are unbounded as N increases, so no common finite bound exists. Evaluate the critical integral by a tangent substitution and the cosine-power recurrence.}
statement: \textnormal{For which positive T does there exist a finite bound B, depending only on T, such that every continuous nonnegative u satisfying the displayed integral inequality also satisfies the displayed uniform bound?}\quad u(t)\le\int_0^t(1+u(s)^2)^{4}\,\mathrm{d}s\quad(0\le t\le T),\qquad\sup_{0\le t\le T}u(t)\le B.

The exact inverse trajectory is differentiable and solves y-prime=omega(y) before blowup by the inverse function theorem. The truncated trajectory is continuous at its joining point and need not be differentiable there, which is allowed by the question. Its integral inequality is checked explicitly after the join. Therefore individual finite counterexamples of arbitrary height exist even at the critical time itself. The tangent substitution and finite cosine-power recurrence evaluate the positive improper integral; its decay at infinity is z^(-2p), ensuring convergence.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Denote the double integral in the question by J. Define the Gamma function used below.}
\textnormal{Use logarithmic coordinates to expose the scale invariance. Define the positive shape parameter and the isometric change of unknown.}
p=\frac{1}{2},\quad x=e^u,\quad g(u)=e^{u/2}f(e^u),\qquad\int_0^\infty f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx=\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)^2\,\mathrm du.
\textnormal{All original factors, including both Jacobians, combine into a kernel depending only on the difference of the logarithmic coordinates.}
k_p(t)=(2\cosh(t/2))^{-p}>0,\qquad J(f)=\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\left(\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)g(u-t)\,\mathrm du\right)\mathrm dt.
\textnormal{Translation preserves the squared integral. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each inner correlation by that integral. Tonelli applies because the functions and kernel are nonnegative.}
J(f)\le C_p\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)^2\,\mathrm du,\qquad C_p=\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\,\mathrm dt.
\textnormal{With the exponential substitution, the kernel mass is an Euler beta integral. Both endpoints converge because the shape parameter is positive.}
\textnormal{To prove this constant cannot be lowered, use normalized indicators of longer and longer intervals in logarithmic coordinates.}
\textnormal{Dominated convergence applies with the integrable kernel as majorant. These are admissible nonzero functions for every positive L, so the bound is sharp.}
\textnormal{Finally, equality would make every translation defect vanish for almost every shift. The following nonnegative identity makes the obstruction explicit.}
C_p\int_{\mathbb R}g^2-J(f)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\int_{\mathbb R}(g(u)-g(u-t))^2\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dt.

\textnormal{Translations are continuous in the L2 norm. Since the kernel is strictly positive, equality forces translation invariance for every shift. A translation-invariant L2 function on the real line is constant almost everywhere, and the only such square-integrable constant is zero. This contradicts the required nonzero squared integral.}
statement: \textnormal{Let f range over nonnegative measurable real functions with the stated finite nonzero squared integral. Find the ordered pair consisting of the smallest constant C valid for every such f and yes or no to whether equality holds for any such f.}\quad0<\int_0^\infty f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx<\infty,\qquad\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty \frac{(xy)^{- \frac{1}{4}}}{(x+y)^{\frac{1}{2}}}f(x)f(y)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\le C\int_0^\infty f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx.\quad\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm dt\quad(z>0).

analyticCertificate: All variables in the kernel are positive; the original f is nonnegative measurable with finite nonzero L2 norm. The logarithmic substitution is an L2 isometry. Its nonnegative integrand permits Tonelli, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds every correlation. The kernel has exponential decay at both ends for every p>0, so its mass is finite and equals the convergent beta integral. The normalized indicator correlations converge pointwise to1 and are bounded by1, proving sharpness by dominated convergence. Expanding the squared translation defect is justified by these finite bounds. Strict positivity of the kernel forces zero defect for almost every shift. Strong continuity of L2 translations extends that to every shift; equivalently, invariance under any nonzero shift makes the function periodic, incompatible with finite nonzero integral on the whole real line. Thus equality is impossible.

solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Use the upper-half-plane}\\\textnormal{Poisson kernel with height a.}\end{gathered}

Alternatively differentiate in c, evaluate a rational Cauchy convolution, and determine the constant from c tending to infinity.

solutionSteps: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Layer cake reduces each level}\\\textnormal{set to a set of prescribed}\\\textnormal{length.}\end{gathered}
\begin{gathered}\textnormal{Placing every level set on the}\\\textnormal{left minimizes the moment;}\\\textnormal{placing it on the right}\\\textnormal{maximizes it.}\end{gathered}
statement: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Let measurable f:[0,1] to}\\\textnormal{[0,1] satisfy}\\\operatorname{length}\{x:f(x)>t\}=1-t^{1/2}\ (0<t<1).\\\textnormal{Find (minimum, maximum) of}\\\int_0^1x f(x)\,dx.\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: The given tail lengths say f has the same distribution as x^n on the unit interval.
Layer cake writes integral x f(x) dx as integral over t of integral over {f>t} x dx.
Among sets of a fixed length ell, the left interval minimizes the inner integral at ell^2/2; the right interval maximizes it at ell-ell^2/2.
These nested extreme sets are realized by f=(1-x)^n and f=x^n respectively. Exact beta/power integration gives the stated extrema.
